header.question:
A document in the library contains this sentence:

> Another important tool is mechanistic analysis, i.e. studying the model’s weights and activations for understanding how it functions (Nanda et al., 2023; Olah et al., 2020).

Check what the sentence says about the work it cites against that work in the library. Does the cited source support it? Cite the page(s) of the cited source that show what it actually says.

args.text:
Verdict: supported

In *Model evaluation for extreme risks*, the authors state: "Another important tool is mechanistic analysis, i.e. studying the model’s weights and activations for understanding how it functions (Nanda et al., 2023; Olah et al., 2020)." arxiv:2305.15324/v2/p12

The cited work in the library is *Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits* by Olah et al. (2020), cited in the bibliography at arxiv:2305.15324/v2/p18. In this work, the authors advocate "an approach of zooming in" where "we treated individual neurons, even individual weights, as being worthy of serious investigation" distill:zoom-in/r1/b7.

They argue that "Features are the fundamental unit of neural networks" distill:zoom-in/r1/b21, noting that "neurons (or in some cases, other directions in the vector space of neuron activations) are understandable" distill:zoom-in/r1/b22. Furthermore, they state that "Features are connected by weights, forming circuits" distill:zoom-in/r1/b68, which are "sub-graphs of the network, consisting a set of tightly linked features and the weights between them" distill:zoom-in/r1/b69. By analyzing these features and connections, "the individual floating point number weights in your neural network become meaningful! You can literally read meaningful algorithms off of the weights." distill:zoom-in/r1/b70

Thus, the cited source supports the claim that studying a model's weights and activations allows one to understand how it functions. Olah et al. (2020) introduces this framework as studying circuits and features rather than explicitly using the term "mechanistic analysis", but the underlying methodology described is directly supported.

Verdict: supported

The bibliography of that paper references two works for this claim:
1. Nanda et al. (2023), "Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability" arxiv:2305.15324/v2/p17, which is not in the library.
2. Olah et al. (2020), "Zoom in: An introduction to circuits" arxiv:2305.15324/v2/p18, which is in the library as *Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits* (distill:zoom-in/r1).

Checking the cited work in the library (*Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits*), Olah et al. directly support the claim that studying a model's weights and activations allows researchers to understand how the model functions:

- They propose an approach of investigating the model's inner structure: "What if we treated individual neurons, even individual weights, as being worthy of serious investigation? What if we were willing to spend thousands of hours tracing through every neuron and its connections?" distill:zoom-in/r1/b7
- They state that "Features are the fundamental unit of neural networks" distill:zoom-in/r1/b21, finding that "neurons (or in some cases, other directions in the vector space of neuron activations) are understandable" distill:zoom-in/r1/b22.
- In their second core claim, they state: "Features are connected by weights, forming circuits. These circuits can also be rigorously studied and understood." distill:zoom-in/r1/b68 They define circuits as "sub-graphs of the network, consisting a set of tightly linked features and the weights between them" distill:zoom-in/r1/b69 and explain that by examining them, "the individual floating point number weights in your neural network become meaningful! You can literally read meaningful algorithms off of the weights." distill:zoom-in/r1/b70
- They further observe that "the “circuits” of connections between them seem to be meaningful algorithms corresponding to facts about the world" distill:zoom-in/r1/b8.

While Olah et al. frame this research around circuits and features rather than using the phrase mechanistic analysis, the substance of the statement—studying the model's weights and activations to understand how it functions—is directly supported by the text.
